quoteEligibleExactSpans: I'm also not losing it it doesn't take very long to replenish a pint of blood
it doesn't require that I have a Divine spark

supportMap.description: Hitchens attributes the rewarding impulse to help others to evolution and denies that it needs divine design or programming.
supportMap.anchor: Evolution has given me for my sake and for everybody else

supportMap.description: Helping for another person's sake produces pleasure alongside humans' predatory and selfish survival traits.
supportMap.anchor: people get pleasure from doing things that aren't necessarily in their interest

supportMap.description: Giving blood transfers life-giving fluid to someone else without lasting loss because a pint is soon replenished.
supportMap.anchor: it doesn't take very long to replenish a pint of blood

supportMap.description: His rare blood group gives him a personal interest in maintaining an adequate shared blood supply for his own future need.
supportMap.anchor: I'm very anxious that there be enough blood when it's my turn

supportMap.description: People vary from donors to sociopaths and psychopaths, a mixture he presents as expected in an imperfectly evolved primate species.
supportMap.anchor: what you would expect from the imperfectly evolved primate species

supportMap.description: The rewarding, reciprocal blood-giving behavior requires neither a divine spark, design, nor programming, while counterexamples fit imperfect evolution.
supportMap.anchor: it doesn't require any design it doesn't require any programming

boundaryJustification.startWhy: Event 2353 begins the first indispensable reason: people feel pleasure when acting for others despite self-interest; events 2359-2360 immediately qualify this by retaining selfish survival traits.
boundaryJustification.endWhy: Event 2402 completes the indispensable conclusion that donors and harmful outliers are unsurprising within an imperfectly evolved primate species.
boundaryJustification.removedPrefix: Events 2343-2352 are removed because they only frame the question as reasoning versus self-sacrifice and announce that an explanation would be desirable; event 2353 begins the actual mechanism.
boundaryJustification.removedSuffix: Events 2403-2411 are removed because the Hitler and Occam's Razor remarks broaden into a separate anti-religious argument after the imperfect-evolution conclusion is already complete at event 2402.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: evolution is a very mixed bag
something is designed uh independent of the morality or goodness or optimality

supportMap.description: Dembski says that accepting evolutionary bonding also admits contrasting evolved conduct, making evolution a morally mixed source rather than a privilege for altruism.
supportMap.anchor: there are lots of other things that you can take as well

supportMap.description: He cites an evolutionary account that treats rape as an adaptation to illustrate evolution's violent side.
supportMap.anchor: argued that rape is an evolutionary adaptation

supportMap.description: He recounts an evolutionary resource-survival explanation of infanticide and connects it to a contemporary case.
supportMap.anchor: mothers would sometimes kill their infants during times of drought

supportMap.description: He summarizes nature as containing both attractive cooperative behavior and wicked behavior, calling evolution a mixed bag.
supportMap.anchor: you'll see some very wicked things

supportMap.description: After conceding natural nastiness as a challenge for design, he distinguishes detecting design from judging its morality, goodness, or optimality.
supportMap.anchor: we can determine whether something is designed uh independent of the morality

supportMap.description: Natural evil challenges design but does not refute it, because design attribution is independent of whether the design is morally good or optimal.
supportMap.anchor: it's a challenge for design but it's not a reputation of design

boundaryJustification.startWhy: Event 2427 begins the operative conditional reply: if bonding is taken from evolution, other evolved behaviors must also be admitted; this directly introduces the mixed-bag argument.
boundaryJustification.endWhy: Event 2487 completes the required design qualification by finishing the phrase that design can be identified independently of its morality, goodness, or optimality.
boundaryJustification.removedPrefix: Events 2413-2426 are removed because they recap Hitchens's bonding theme and offer divine design as another possible origin; the actual criticism of evolutionary moral selection starts at event 2427.
boundaryJustification.removedSuffix: Events 2488-2497 are removed because they add closing remarks about the discussion's depth and repeat that evolutionary morality is a mixed bag after the conclusion is complete at event 2487.

repairs.longerCompleteArgumentRationale: Events 2427-2434 frame the inference from evolutionary bonding to other evolved conduct; 2435-2454 provide the separated rape and infanticide examples; 2455-2462 draw the mixed-bag point; and 2463-2487 develop Darwin's natural-evil concern, concede it as a challenge for design, and conclude that it is not a refutation because design detection is independent of moral goodness or optimality. The intervening material is needed to connect those named examples and the required concession to the concluding distinction.

limitations: The assigned source is an automatic-caption excerpt; several names and words are visibly mistranscribed, so quotation candidates avoid those garbled phrases.
